“Check your analytics” is useless advice until you know which tool answers which question. Telegram has three analytics layers, and confusing them wastes money and weeks. Here’s the comparison by use case.
What it is:
the reference analytics + catalog service for public channels. Anyone can look up any channel.
Key numbers:
average post reach,
ERR
(engagement rate per reach — views vs subscribers), subscriber dynamics,
citation index
(how often other channels link you).
Use it for:
vetting swap partners, benchmarking your niche, being vetted by advertisers. Your TGStat page is your public credit report.
Limitation:
public aggregates only — no per-hour view curves for your own decision-making.
the second major analytics/catalog platform, strongest on
ad analytics
: which channels run whose ads, price estimates, audience overlap.
pricing your ad inventory, checking a channel’s ad history before buying, competitive recon in your niche.
same as TGStat’s — public-facing, aggregate.
per-post analytics from the tool that actually publishes for you. ControllerBot reports views and engagement per post;
charts view dynamics per post plus sends and channel history.
the questions that matter weekly — which slot performs, which content shape gets first-hour views, what to make more of.
your channel only; no market context.

For the discussion group: member activity, reputation, top commenters, moderation history. Group health predicts channel retention — a thriving comment section shows up in Combot before it shows anywhere else.
“Should I swap with this channel?” → TGStat/Telemetr.
“What should I post Tuesday?” → scheduler stats.
“What do I charge for an ad?” → Telemetr comps + your TGStat ERR.
“Is my community healthy?” → Combot.
“When should I post?” → your scheduler’s first-hour curves (native stats are too coarse).

ERR (engagement rate of reach — views ÷ subscribers, usually on the last several posts) is the number everyone quotes and few calibrate. Rules of thumb admins actually trade on: under 1,000 subscribers, a healthy channel posts ERR of 50% and up — small audiences are loyal audiences; 1,000–10,000, the 25–45% band is normal and 30%+ is strong; above 50,000, mature channels live in the 10–25% range and anything higher is suspiciously good. Two calibration rules matter more than the thresholds.
Compare within your niche:
a deals channel's ERR runs structurally lower than a micro-lessons channel's — the number only means something next to its own species.
Watch the trend, not the value:

an ERR sliding from 32% to 24% over a quarter is the loudest retention alarm you have; a stable 18% is a fine, honest channel. Advertisers price on ERR because it's the closest thing to "how many real humans see this" — keeping yours honest keeps every future negotiation honest too.
Analytics that doesn't end in a decision is procrastination with charts. The ritual that fits in a coffee break:
pull the last seven posts' views and compute views ÷ subscribers — the ERR trend line;
note the best and worst post of the week and write one sentence on why (format? topic? time?) — this is where the editorial instinct gets data;
check joins vs leaves for the week, and if leaves spiked, find the post that caused it;
check forwards and reactions on the top post — the formats worth repeating;

glance at the scheduler's upcoming queue and confirm next week exists. Five numbers, five minutes of notes, one decision: what next week gets more of and less of. The ritual compounds precisely because it's boring — channels that "check stats when curious" get curious twice a quarter.

Per-post link attribution is the weakest link in the Telegram analytics chain, and knowing its edges prevents bad decisions. Channel posts are forwarded and re-viewed for months, so click counts accumulate slowly and a "flop" post at 48 hours can be the quarter's best click-source at day 60 — judge link posts on a 30-day window. UTMs work fine (Telegram's in-app browser preserves parameters), but they don't survive screenshots and re-typing, which is where promo codes earn their keep: a code is attribution that travels by word of mouth. Shortlinks you control (a branded short domain) let you recount clicks later and see the decay curve; raw destination URLs hide it. And when comparing channels for paid promos, remember the numbers asymmetry: TGStat estimates views publicly, but clicks on your own links are the only number you can fully trust — which is why serious sponsors ask for a test post with a tracked link before any bundle deal.
Common questions
What is ERR in TGStat?
Engagement Rate per Reach — average post views relative to subscriber count. It normalizes channel size so a 3K channel can be compared honestly with a 300K one. Above 30% is strong in most niches.
Do I need paid analytics for a small channel?
No — TGStat’s free lookups cover vetting and benchmarking, and your scheduler’s built-in stats cover daily decisions. Paid tiers matter once you trade ad inventory seriously.
Why do TGStat numbers differ from my channel’s stats?
They sample and average differently (time windows, post selection). Both are honest; use TGStat for public comparison and your scheduler’s numbers for operational decisions.
Which Telegram analytics shows who viewed my post?
None — Telegram doesn’t expose individual viewers. Views are anonymous counts; the deepest public signal is the view curve over time, which scheduling bots chart per post.
